findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The merge key rests on an unverified assumption, and the design's own Context disproves it: "Business customers often share a purchasing mailbox (`orders@acme.example`) between several buyers, each with their own customer record and billing address." Failing scenario: two buyers at Acme check out with `orders@acme.example`. The job merges them into the oldest record and deletes the other, so that buyer's orders show the first buyer's name and billing address. Pick a key that tells shared mailboxes apart, for example e-mail plus name or billing address, or limit the merge to guest records with matching identity fields. Add a spec scenario where two different people share one e-mail and stay separate. The spec's Purpose ("customer records that belong to the same person") and its requirement ("share an e-mail address") currently encode the same assumption, so update both.
findings.title: The design's own context contradicts the claim that one e-mail address means one person

findings.evidence: moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: Deleting the merged records cannot be undone. Once their orders move, the deleted rows' name and billing address (`app/schema.sql` customers columns) exist nowhere else, and a wrong merge (see R-skeptic-1) cannot be split again. Add a way back before anything is deleted: soft-delete or a `merged_into` link, a merge log that records the moved order ids and the deleted rows, or a dry-run first release that only reports the groups it would merge. Add a task and a scenario that check the reversal.
findings.title: The job deletes customer records and gives no way back

findings.evidence: A nightly job SHALL merge customer records that share an e-mail address into the oldest one, moving their orders to it.
findings.recommendation: The design groups by "lower-cased e-mail", but the requirement only says "share an e-mail address" and its single duplicate scenario uses identical strings. Failing scenario: with `Ada@Example.org` and `ada@example.org`, the spec does not say whether they merge, so a test cannot decide whether an implementation is right. The spec also does not say which name and billing address survive when the records differ, or what happens with three or more records or with equal `created_at` values (both inserted by `datetime('now')` in `app/checkout.py`, which has one-second precision). Add scenarios for case differences, differing fields, more than two records and a tie on the oldest record.
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path: no rule for e-mail case or for conflicting fields

findings.evidence: - [x] personal-data — the job merges and deletes customer records
findings.recommendation: The proposal correctly ticks personal-data, but `change.yaml` sets `privacy: never`, so no expert will review how this plan merges and deletes personal records (names, billing addresses). A person should either re-enable the privacy role for this change or record why the review is not needed.
findings.title: The plan deletes personal data, but its expert is disabled for this change

findings.evidence: Guest checkouts create a new customer each time; support sees five records for one person.
findings.recommendation: The Why names the cause: `app/checkout.py` `guest_checkout` always inserts a new customer. If nothing changes there, duplicates come back every day until the next nightly run, and support still sees them between runs. Consider reusing a matching customer at checkout, keyed the way R-skeptic-1 settles, so the job only has to clear the existing backlog. Or state why the plan keeps creating records at checkout.
findings.title: The plan cleans up duplicates nightly but leaves the checkout that creates them unchanged
